children.title: Federal Agencies Cancel About $400 Million in Columbia Grants and Contracts
children.description_short: On March 7, 2025, federal agencies announced cancellation of about $400 million in grants and contracts to Columbia University.
children.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, four federal agencies announced the immediate cancellation of approximately $400 million in grants and contracts to Columbia University. The Justice Department called it an initial round and tied the action to alleged failures to address harassment of Jewish students. Reuters reported that the government did not specify the affected grants or its evidence. This was a Columbia action, not a blanket three-university cutoff.
children.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the Departments of Justice, Health and Human Services, Education, and the General Services Administration announced the immediate cancellation of approximately $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University. The Justice Department said it was the first round of action and tied the cancellations to what the administration described as Columbia’s inaction over harassment of Jewish students. Reuters reported that the administration did not identify which grants or contracts were affected or disclose its evidence for the stated rationale. This card describes a specific action against Columbia; it does not claim that every federal research or education dollar to the university ended. The sources also do not show a simultaneous action against Harvard and Yale. The supplied parent entry placed Columbia in an August 2025 three-university cutoff, but the documented Columbia action occurred in March and is distinct from the later Harvard action. The administration’s stated justification is attributed here, not presented as a judicial finding.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

children.title: Administration Freezes $2.2 Billion in Harvard Grants and $60 Million in Contracts
children.description_short: On April 14, 2025, the administration announced a freeze on $2.2 billion in Harvard grants and $60 million in multi-year contract value.
children.description_medium: On April 14, 2025, after Harvard rejected administration demands, the Trump administration announced a freeze on $2.2 billion in multi-year grants and $60 million in multi-year contract value. The Education Department described it as a freeze. Reuters reported Harvard said the demands would cede university control and threatened academic freedom. This action concerned Harvard alone, not a joint three-university funding cutoff.
children.description_long: On April 14, 2025, Harvard rejected administration demands and the Trump administration announced a freeze on $2.2 billion in multi-year grants plus $60 million in multi-year contract value. The Department of Education described the action as a freeze; Reuters reported that it came within hours of Harvard’s rejection and said the university viewed the demands as ceding control and threatening academic freedom. This card concerns the announced action against Harvard alone. It does not show that every federal research and education fund was ended, that Yale was included, or that a simultaneous August action occurred. The administration attributed its decision to civil-rights concerns and campus antisemitism; those are its stated rationales, not independent findings established by these sources. The official announcement specifies multi-year grant and contract value, not all current or future federal money. The parent entry merged this April event with Columbia’s separate March cancellations and claimed a broader three-university cutoff.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: April 14, 2025. Today, the Joint Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism released the following statement: “Harvard’s statement today reinforces the troubling entitlement mindset that is endemic in our nation’s most prestigious universities and colleges – that federal investment does not come with the responsibility to uphold civil rights laws. The disruption of learning that has plagued campuses in recent years is unacceptable. The harassment of Jewish students is intolerable. It is time for elite universities to take the problem seriously and commit to meaningful change if they wish to continue receiving taxpayer support. The Joint Task Force to combat anti-Semitism is announcing a freeze on $2.2 billion in multi-year grants and $60M in multi-year contract value to Harvard University.”

terminal_record.title: DOJ Narrows One Proposed Google Antitrust Remedy While Continuing the Case
terminal_record.description_short: DOJ dropped its proposed requirement for Google to divest AI investments while continuing to seek Chrome divestiture in its search case.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department revised its proposed remedy in the Google search-monopoly case. Reuters reported that DOJ no longer sought mandatory divestiture of Google’s AI investments, instead seeking advance notice of future generative-AI investments. DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued to seek Chrome divestiture and other measures. The filing changed one proposed remedy; it did not end the case or establish a final court outcome.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department filed a revised proposal in the federal search-monopoly case against Google. Reuters reported that DOJ dropped its proposed requirement that Google sell its investments in artificial-intelligence companies, including Anthropic, and shifted to requiring advance notice of future investments in generative AI. The same report said DOJ and 38 state attorneys general still sought a court order requiring Google to divest its Chrome browser and take other measures addressing the search monopoly a judge had found. This was a change to proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case. The filing left major remedies in dispute; it did not establish that any remedy had taken effect or that DOJ abandoned the action as a whole. The source describes a formal litigation proposal and attributes it to court papers filed in Washington. The supplied packet’s claim that the department dropped the case, or did so in exchange for donations, is not supported by this evidence and is omitted. Timing and campaign donations do not establish motive. The court’s final remedy and the case’s later disposition are outside the verified facts in this card.
